quotes.quote: The Victoria Cross (VC) is Britain’s highest award for gallantry.
The decoration takes the form of a cross pattée, 1.375 inches (35mm) wide, bearing a crown surmounted by a lion and the inscription ‘For Valour’.
There is no barrier of colour, creed, sex or rank. Indeed, VC recipients have come from all social backgrounds and from across the British Empire and Commonwealth.
The Victoria Cross (VC) was awarded 628 times to 627 recipients for action in the First World War (1914–1918).
account for almost half the 1356 Victoria Crosses awarded throughout its history; in comparison the Second World War saw 181 medals awarded.

The VC was instituted by Royal Warrant on 29 January 1856 to acknowledge the bravery displayed by many soldiers and sailors during the Crimean War (1854-56). Unlike its predecessors, the new award was open to all ranks and would only be granted for acts of supreme gallantry in the face of the enemy.
The first 85 awards - announced in 'The London Gazette' of 24 February 1857 - were made retrospectively, dating back to the start of the Crimean campaign in the autumn of 1854.
This eligibility was further extended to all colonial and auxiliary troops in 1881.
The Royal Warrant of 21 October 1911, published in 'The London Gazette' on 12 December, extended VC eligibility to Indian soldiers.
The historian John Glanfield has established that the metal for most of the medals made since December 1914 came from two Chinese cannon and that there is no evidence of Russian origin.

quotes.quote: A recommendation for the VC was normally issued by an officer at regiment or ship level, and had to be supported by three witnesses. From there, it was passed up the military hierarchy until it reached first the Secretary of State for War, and then the monarch.

The original Royal Warrant made no mention of posthumous awards. It had been decided from the outset that the VC would not be awarded for an act in which the individual was killed, or where he died shortly after.
In 1900, during the Boer War (1899-1902), a posthumous VC was awarded to Lieutenant Frederick Roberts of the King’s Royal Rifle Corps.
Posthumous VCs continued to be awarded during the First World War (1914-18), but it was not until 1920 that specific provision for such cases was formally established by Royal Warrant.

Major Arthur Martin-Leake was awarded the VC for his actions on 8 February 1902 while serving as a surgeon with the South African Constabulary at Vlakfontein during the Boer War (1899–1902). He received a bar to his cross for bravery between 29 October and 8 November 1914 near Zonnebeke on the Western Front. Captain Noel Chavasse of the Royal Army Medical Corps was awarded the VC for his actions on 9 August 1916 at Guillemont on the Somme, and a posthumous bar for gallantry between 31 July and 2 August 1917 at Wieltje in Flanders.
